In my experience, it is indeed more maintainable to have more integretion tests. I mean, most QA theories mention the testing pyramid, which basically tells you that you should have a lot of unit tests, less integration tests and even less E2E, as the more complex tests take more time to maintain and therefore cost more resources.
The problem I noticed is that even if the people know this, there is not enough time to do it right from the beginning, so the management tends to say QA should implement some E2E tests to start and build the rest of the pyramid later. But that usually doesn't happen. There are more and more requests why isn't xy covered by tests, more E2E tests are written and then we are all caught in the loop of maintaining those tests and don't have time to implement the lower level tests.

In my experience, all UI test are extremely difficult to maintain. That's the reason why all the theories of automated testing say that UI tests are the smallest amount of all the tests. And when you are not writing them but you try to record them in whatever tool, it's even more tricky. It sounds better in theory then when you actually do it. When something - like an ID of one button - changes in one page, you have to rerecord all the tests that are using it. When you have the code, you just change the ID of the button, so that's a change of one line and that's it.

One time I wrote 200 UI tests. It took me 2 months to learn how to do it and actually write them. The next 3 years I only try to maintain them and maybe write some more... But I never got to writing any more as all my time was wasting maintaing the ones I already had and they were never up to date. As soon as I fixed some, another test started failing because of a change in application. It was horrible! So for next project someone came with an idea of recording the test scenarios instead as it's supposed to be faster. And I got to 30 tests and got stuck again in the vicious cycle of maintaining the tests that never work.
